title: An absolutely unorderable nontrivial combinatory algebra
formal: Does a combinatory algebra A with at least two elements exist such that every combinatory algebra B admitting an embedding of A has only the equality relation as a compatible partial order?
definitions: A combinatory algebra consists of a set, a total binary application operation and distinguished elements K,S satisfying (Kx)y=x and ((Sx)y)z=(xz)(yz) for all x,y,z. Parentheses specify the application order. An embedding is an injective map preserving application and both distinguished elements. A compatible partial order is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive relation ≤ such that x≤x′ and y≤y′ imply xy≤x′y′. The target quantifies over B of arbitrary cardinality and every such embedding. No countability, effectiveness or additional extensionality axiom is required.

context_blocks.text: Order-theoretic models underlie much of the semantics of untyped computation. Absolute unorderability would exhibit an algebra whose equations cannot be faithfully retained inside any nontrivially ordered combinatory model.

Selinger distinguishes unorderability of one algebra from the stronger prohibition on all embeddings into ordered extensions. The former does not answer the latter: an algebra with only a discrete compatible order can still embed in an orderable extension. The target is the combinatory-algebra version explicitly stated in the source.

why: Test a foundational limitation of order-theoretic semantics for universal untyped computation.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
